Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of witnessed childhood domestic violence. Explosion/bang sounds, medical equipment/needles, and nature-based reminders point toward very different trauma contexts (combat/blast, medical trauma, outdoor assault/disaster) rather than a single domestic-violence witnessing history. This is a hard-to-explain mismatch within the Triggers node and also weakly linked to the selected Memory and Maladaptive Strategies items, which do not anchor these disparate cues to one coherent trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed domestic violence in childhood. Doors slamming is plausible, but medical equipment/needles and being in a natural environment suggest very different trauma contexts and are hard to reconcile with the same index trauma without additional explanation.

issues.item: Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'photographic recall' and 'hard to recall deliberately' pull in opposing directions. A patient may have fragmented trauma memory, but endorsing vividly photographic recall while also saying the memory is difficult to deliberately access is a direct tension that is clinically questionable as a paired summary of the same trauma memory profile.

Within the Memory node, 'Photographic Recall' and 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' pull in opposite directions if both are intended as general descriptions of the same trauma memory. Vivid, photograph-like recall can coexist with patchy retrieval, but paired without any qualifier it is clinically tense enough to question coherence.

The trigger set does not cohere well with the stated trauma of witnessed childhood domestic violence. 'Doors opening or slamming' and 'Alcohol smell' are plausible domestic-violence cues, but 'Being in Nature' is hard to link to this trauma type unless unusual contextual details are present.

Cross-node coherence is weakened because the trigger profile mixes highly domestic/interpersonal cues (door slamming, alcohol smell) with 'Being in Nature,' while the memory items do not provide a contextual bridge explaining why a natural environment would cue this trauma.

vignette:
Kofi is a 79-year-old African American man, divorced, who has spent the last several years working warehouse shifts - moving inventory, loading pallets, operating in the low hum of fluorescent light and diesel - a life built, he would say, around keeping busy. He came to the clinic after his supervisor referred him following a workplace incident in which Kofi became agitated and combative during a routine break, apparently triggered by nothing his coworkers could identify. He arrived for his first session guarded but willing, and what emerged over the following weeks was a clinical picture rooted not in a single adult crisis but in something far older and far less fully formed in his memory.

Kofi grew up in a rural setting - fields, tree lines, the smell of damp earth and wood smoke - and it was in that environment, as a young child, that he witnessed sustained and severe domestic violence between his parents. He cannot reconstruct it cleanly. What he has are pieces: a door swinging open hard against a wall, the particular smell of his father's breath, a feeling of cold ground beneath him, the sound of something breaking. He does not have a narrative. He has fragments that do not connect to one another and, when he tries deliberately to sit with what happened, the memory recedes - he reaches for it and finds only blankness or a sudden, overwhelming wave of feeling he cannot attach to any image. This quality of the memory - its fragmentation, its resistance to deliberate recall, the way emotion arrives without content - means that Kofi has spent most of his adult life uncertain of what, precisely, he is carrying.

What the memory cannot deliver consciously, the body and the environment deliver without warning. On days when Kofi's warehouse work takes him to the loading dock at the edge of the property, where scrubland and open sky are visible beyond the fence, something shifts in him that he cannot name but cannot ignore. Natural settings - the particular quality of open land, the smell of vegetation - reach back across seven decades and pull. A door slamming in the warehouse, the kind of sharp percussive bang that happens dozens of times a shift, can stop him mid-step. The smell of alcohol on a colleague's breath during a break has, more than once, sent him outside shaking. These fragments of the environment act as keys to something the memory itself has sealed shut, and the distress they produce is immediate and physical, arriving before any thought has formed.

When those moments come, Kofi's response has, over decades, settled into a set of strategies that feel to him like management but function as maintenance. He drinks - not heavily by his own accounting, though the clinic's screening suggests otherwise - and he has come to rely on over-the-counter sleep aids in combination. He picks arguments. At work, at home before his marriage ended, with strangers in parking lots - conflict, he has learned, floods the system with something sharp and present that crowds out whatever was threatening to surface. He keeps himself surrounded by people whenever possible, filling evenings with neighbours, acquaintances, anyone who will sit with him, because silence and solitude are where the feelings find him. But the alcohol, in particular, has begun to work against him in a way he is only now acknowledging: it blurs the already fragmented memory further, leaving him with even less access to what happened, which means the fragments that do break through feel more alien, more uncontrollable, more likely to erupt in response to the next door slam or the next stretch of open field. The strategies that were meant to manage the triggers have, over time, eroded the very memory structures that might have allowed him to locate and contain what he is reacting to - and so the triggers retain their full, disorienting power.

The workplace incident was the thing that finally moved him. He had shoved a younger colleague after a door slammed, and the shame of that - at 79, a man who had worked hard to be steady - was, he said, worse than anything else. He does not know exactly what he is hoping for. He suspects he may never have a clear account of what happened in that house. What he wants, he said quietly at the end of the second session, is to stop being ambushed by a past he cannot even properly see.
